title: Learned Execution Graphs for Anomaly Detection & Drift in APIs — Ritvik Pandya, JP Morgan Chase

summary: Ritvik Pandya introduces learned execution graphs as short-lived DAGs representing the full path of each API request through middleware (edge, gateway, ingress, auth, orchestration, parallel systems, client notification), with loops and retries modeled as separate entities. The core method is: represent request processing as a DAG, establish baselines, detect deviation, localize the problem node, compare against threshold, and act only when deviation is significant. A cheap tier-one check (the 'boarding pass' analogy) lets most requests skip deeper analysis; only detected drift escalates to tier-two investigation of structural changes, scale deviations, divergence, and per-client baselines. The talk distinguishes anomaly (one-off incident like a traffic jam) from drift (slow baseline shift like commute time growing over a year). Drift is categorized into structural (new/removed step), volume (service overwhelmed by request volume), and covariate/behavioral (changing request mix, e.g., more international requests needing currency conversion). The pipeline uses OpenTelemetry feeding traces asynchronously via Kafka, with a hot path for fast decisions and a recon path for accurate analysis. Benchmarking used OpenTelemetry and StarBench with millions of traces over 7 days, injecting anomalies before training. Tuning challenges include delayed events (tail-based tracking to avoid false structural-change alarms), sampling, and cold starts (new endpoints need own baselines). Results show mean time to discovery reduced significantly by using single-window rather than multi-window comparison. Key lessons include using granular per-use-case baselines (e.g., separate baselines for real-time payments vs. wire payments), ensuring well-defined per-client windows for structural changes, providing explainability so outputs are actionable (health score analogy), and keeping the system aware of new deployments so rollback decisions can be made. Admin confirmation and classification precede any automated remediation, with gradual rollout at 5-10% before 100%.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Execution graphs are short-lived DAGs of a request's middleware steps, distinct from persistent/property graphs.
Method flow: represent request as DAG, baseline, detect deviation, localize node, compare to threshold, act only if needed.
Anomaly is a one-off incident; drift is a slow baseline shift requiring a new baseline; three drift types: structural, volume, covariate/behavioral.
Per-node baselines enable precise localization of performance problems to the exact node instead of the whole endpoint.
Use granular per-use-case baselines (real-time payments vs. wire payments) rather than one generic baseline per HTTP method.
Single-window comparison dramatically reduced mean time to discovery versus waiting across multiple time windows.
Explainability is essential: raw scores without context are unactionable; data should be well explained for informed decisions.
The system must be deployment-aware so rollback decisions can be made when new deployments introduce issues.
Gradual rollout of fixes: 5-10% of machines first, monitor, then 100%.
Distinguish persistent graphs from short-lived execution graphs

sections.title: Execution graphs for anomaly and drift detection
sections.summary: Introduction of the speaker and the concept of execution graphs as short-lived graphs for detecting anomalies and drift, contrasted with persistent/property graphs.

sections.title: What a short lived execution graph is
sections.summary: Defines execution graph as a DAG representing request processing through edge, gateways, ingress, auth, orchestration, parallel systems, and client notification; loops/retries modeled as separate entities.

sections.title: Tiered checks and per client baselines
sections.summary: Tier-one cheap check (boarding pass analogy) skips deeper analysis unless baseline deviation is found; per-client baselines account for differences like local vs. external requests, reducing alert noise.

sections.title: The method: baseline, deviation, localize, act
sections.summary: Core method: represent request as DAG, establish baseline, detect deviation, localize problem node, compare to threshold, act only if outside threshold.

sections.title: Localizing a slow node, and how the system is trained
sections.summary: Example localizing slow FX rate node; benchmarking via OpenTelemetry and StarBench over 7 days with millions of traces and injected anomalies for pre-live training.

sections.title: Anomaly versus drift
sections.summary: Anomaly is a one-off incident (traffic jam analogy); drift is a slow baseline shift (commute time growing over a year) requiring a new baseline.

sections.title: The three kinds of drift: structural, volume, covariate
sections.summary: Structural drift: added/removed nodes (coffee shop membership analogy); volume drift: service overloaded by request volume; covariate/behavioral drift: changing request mix (e.g., more international requests needing currency conversion) requiring reassessed baselines or separate graphs.

sections.title: The pipeline: from telemetry to gradual rollout
sections.summary: OpenTelemetry feeds data; root cause analysis identifies drift type and solution; risk assessment; gradual rollout at 5-10% then 100% after verification.

sections.title: Hot path versus recon, and worked examples
sections.summary: Hot path for fast decisions, recon path for accurate analysis; example localizing slow node in 700ms request; async OpenTelemetry via Kafka; contrast node-specific vs. system-wide delay.

sections.title: Tuning it: delayed events, sampling, cold starts
sections.summary: Tuning challenges: delayed events may look like structural change (use tail-based tracking), cold starts need new endpoint baselines, detection via MMD or KL divergence, admin confirmation before classification and automation.

sections.title: Results and lessons
sections.summary: Single-window comparison reduced mean time to discovery to near real-time. Lessons: use granular per-use-case baselines (real-time payments vs. wire payments) rather than one per HTTP method; define well-structured windows per client for structural changes; new baselines reduce noise; explainability is essential (health score analogy—raw numbers without context are unactionable); system must be deployment-aware to enable rollback decisions.

demonstrations: Example DAG: edge layer → gateways → ingress → auth/authz → orchestration → parallel systems → client notification
Benchmarking pipeline using OpenTelemetry and StarBench with 7 days of millions of injected traces

limitations: Delayed telemetry events can cause false structural-change alarms, requiring tail-based tracking and tuning
Cold starts for new endpoints need separate baselines, not generic ones
Labels help but system requires careful fine-tuning
One generic baseline per HTTP method is insufficient; per-use-case baselines needed
Statistical approach is one module of a larger neuro-specific system, not the whole solution
